title: Why the rich borrow money and the poor pay it back

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Same day, two loans. Five years on, his car is worth {carval_final}. Ten years on, her house could be worth {home_final}.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: I just signed for my dream car. Only {car_emi} a month!

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And I signed for a mortgage. Thirty years of payments. Ugh.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Both of them borrowed. But only one of them borrowed the way the rich do.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: People think the rich hate debt. We love it. We just never use it the way you do.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So here are five kinds of debt you are likely to carry, the one question that sorts good from bad, and why the most expensive loan is the one that looks cheapest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's car costs {car_amount}. The bank lends him all of it, at {car_rate} a year, for six years.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: And the payment is just {car_emi}. I can totally afford that.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Just? Rohan, how long is just?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Six years. And then it's all mine. Everyone I know has a car loan anyway.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Everybody can afford the payment, beta. Ask what the car costs you.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Yes. And everyone you know says they are broke.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan isn't foolish. The monthly payment is the only number anyone ever showed him.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The dealer shows him a shiny car and one small monthly number. Here's what that number hides.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: {car_months} payments of {car_emi} add up to {car_total_paid}. And {car_interest} of that is pure interest.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Okay, some interest. But at least I own a really nice car now.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A car starts losing value the day it leaves the lot. Assume it loses fifteen percent a year. After five years, his is worth {carval_final}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So after five years, he has paid a lot, and he owns a car worth less than half its price. Here is the damage.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He borrowed {carloss_a}. The car has already lost {carloss_diff} of it.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So the loan bought something that shrinks. And he pays interest the whole time it shrinks.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Wait. I'm paying the bank to watch my car get cheaper?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Exactly. That is debt working against you. Every month, a little more of your pay walks out the door.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But I need a car to get to work.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Sure. But needing a car and needing that car are two very different things.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's the first difference. The poor borrow for things that lose value. The rich borrow for things that gain it.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Rich people buy cars too. Usually with money they've already made, and often a cheaper car than they could afford.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And a car loan, at least, ends. The next debt can follow you for {card_years} years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It started with one dinner he couldn't quite afford. Then a jacket on sale. Then a trip with friends.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's card has a balance of {card_amount}. The interest rate is {card_rate_year} a year.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: No problem. The app says I only have to pay {card_min_due} this month.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But I pay every single month. I'm never late!

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Paying on time keeps the late fees away. It doesn't touch the interest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The minimum is a small slice of the balance. At first, most of it goes straight to interest.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: A low minimum feels kind. But the longer you take to pay, the more interest the bank earns.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Picture a bucket with a hole. He pours in {card_min_due} a month, and interest leaks most of it straight back out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: After a whole year of payments, he still owes {card_owed_year1}.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: I have seen this film before. It runs for {card_years} years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Paying only the minimum, his balance crawls toward zero for {card_years} years.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: {card_years} years? I'll have kids in school by then!

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The interest alone adds up to {card_interest}. More than the whole balance he borrowed.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So the card bought dinners and a jacket. And he's still paying for them years later.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: The jacket is already out of fashion!

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Rich people use cards too. They pay the full statement every month, and the bank earns nothing from them in interest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So that's two debts. A car that shrinks and a card that never ends. Next, the debt the rich actually like.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Priya buys a home for {home_amount}. She puts some savings down, and borrows {mortgage_amount}.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Thirty years at {mortgage_rate}. That's {mortgage_emi} every month. A lot of payments.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Why didn't she just keep renting? No mortgage, no stress.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Rent buys me a place to live this month. A mortgage payment also buys me a little more of the house.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here's the honest number first. Over thirty years, the bank collects {mortgage_interest} in interest.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That's way more interest than my car! So she's worse off than me?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Not so fast. Look at what her loan bought.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Assume homes in her town grow {home_rate} a year. That's an assumption, not a promise.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Ten years later, her house could be worth {home_final}.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Could be? So it might not be?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Could be. That's the honest word. Nobody knows what house prices will do next.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: That's {home_gains} more than the price. And that growth is mine, not the bank's.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The bank gets its interest. She gets the growth on the whole house, not just on the part she paid.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's called leverage. Borrow most of the price, and the whole thing grows for you.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Notice what each of them signed for. Rohan, a car that loses value every year. Priya, a house that can gain value.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here's the second difference. The rich borrow at low rates. The poor borrow at high ones.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And she pays {mortgage_rate}, while his card charges {card_rate_year}. Cheap money is the rich person's favourite tool.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Banks charge less when a loan is backed by something valuable, like a house.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: And my card is backed by... a jacket.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The catch: a house also costs taxes, insurance and repairs. And prices can fall. In some years, they did.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So a house can make you richer. But it's not free money.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Right. The question is never the monthly payment. It's what the loan buys.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: His car payment buys a ride. My mortgage payment buys a roof, and a little more of the house every month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the next loan doesn't buy a thing you can touch at all. It buys a skill.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Priya's cousin borrows {school_amount} for a degree, at {school_rate}, over ten years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's {school_emi} a month, and {school_interest} in interest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: About the same interest as Rohan's car loan. But a very different bet.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So it's just another loan, like my car.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: It depends on one thing. What does the course do to the salary?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: If the degree lifts her pay by more than {school_emi} a month, the loan pays for itself, and then some.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And if it doesn't, it's a car loan with a diploma.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: A car loan with a diploma. Okay, I'm stealing that one.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Before I signed anything, I asked what people with that degree actually earn.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan took an online course once too. He never asked what it would pay him back.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: If a course can't tell you what its students go on to earn, that's your answer.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: What course was it, Rohan?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: How to get rich from home. It had really good reviews.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The skill loan is the one rich people take most happily: a loan on themselves. But only when the numbers say it pays.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A skill can't be repossessed, and it can't lose value sitting in a parking lot.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So before the next course, I check what it pays first. Got it.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Good. That one habit puts you ahead before you borrow a cent.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So that's four debts. Two bought things that shrink. Two bought things that can grow.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Next, the one question that sorts every loan you will ever take.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Before any loan, I ask one thing. Does it pay me, or do I pay it?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So compare two numbers. What the debt costs a year, and what the money could earn a year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's card costs {card_rate_year} a year. Assume a broad stock market fund returns {six_rate} a year over the long run.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Paying off that card is like earning {card_rate_year} on your money. No fund promises you that.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So clearing my card is the best deal I've got?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: That's why rich people rarely carry a card balance. That debt only ever pays the bank.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Her mortgage costs {mortgage_rate}. Her home, if it grows {home_rate} a year, gives her growth on the whole price.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On paper, the interest costs her a bit more than the growth. But she also gets a place to live, and a fixed payment that does not rise with rent.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now run every loan through that one question.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Card: I pay it. Car: I pay it. Her house: it can pay her. The degree: it depends.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: If the borrowed money earns more than its rate, the debt works for you. If not, you work for the debt.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And Rohan's car loan? It costs {car_rate} a year, for a thing that loses value every year. It fails the question twice.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So here's most of the rule. Cheap debt, for things that can grow. No debt, for things that shrink.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So what should I do with my card right now?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: We don't tell anyone what to do. But you can run the question yourself, on every loan you have.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But there's one debt that looks cheaper than all of them. And many people carry it their whole lives.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Six years later, Rohan finally pays off the car. So what does he do next?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: New car! Same payment, new smell.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Many people always have a car payment. One loan ends, and the next one starts.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So what if the same {car_emi} went into investments instead, every month?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Investments? Isn't that only for people who are already rich?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: It's how a lot of people become rich. Slowly, with ordinary amounts like this one.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At an assumed {six_rate} a year, six years of that payment grows to {six_final}.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And that is from just one car.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That's more than the whole car cost me!

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now keep it going for thirty years, the way many people keep a car payment.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Okay. How much are we talking?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Thirty years of that payment, invested, becomes {life_final}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Not because the payment was big. Because it never stopped, and it had thirty years to grow.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He would have put in {life_invested}. The other {life_gains} is growth.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And that's with no stock tips and no luck. Just a payment that stayed home every month.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: That is the payment people call cheap.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: All of that, parked in my driveway.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: To be fair, you still need a car. But a cheaper one, kept longer, frees up most of that payment.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And markets don't go up in a straight line. {six_rate} is an assumption, and some years will be down.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: At your age, I rode a scooter, not a new car. And every month, I paid myself the car payment instead.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Wait. Is that why you live in a penthouse?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: That, and a lot of patience.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So, five debts. A car and a card that shrink. A house and a skill that can grow. And a payment that never ends.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: So here is how the rich borrow. Cheap money, for things that pay them back.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Okay. Next car: a cheaper one, and I keep it longer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the poor borrow expensive money for things that don't. Does your loan pay you, or do you pay it?
Our maths is simplified: before tax, fees and upkeep, with assumed growth rates. Good debt or bad debt? Tell us which one you have.

params.assumption: Assumes car loan {car_rate}, car value {carval_rate} a year, card {card_rate_year} paying the minimum, homes {home_rate} a year, market {six_rate} a year; before tax, fees and upkeep.
